title: When Building Goes Wrong: Microcephaly, Zika and Lissencephaly

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Which cortical progenitor cells both produce neurons and provide fibers for their outward migration?
cards.back: Radial glia.
cards.quote: Radial glia, the progenitor cells that line the fluid-filled ventricle, divide to make more of themselves and then to make neurons
cards.section: Number or place

cards.front: A cluster of neurons sitting where they do not belong is a {{c1::heterotopia}}.
cards.back: The neurons were made but misplaced.
cards.quote: a heterotopia: a cluster of neurons sitting where they do not belong.
cards.section: Number or place

cards.front: Why can an early progenitor-division defect affect more neurons than the stalling of one migrating neuron?
cards.back: A division defect reduces a multiplying progenitor pool and its future output. A stalled neuron takes no descendants with it.
cards.quote: The second job does not multiply: a neuron that stalls is one neuron in the wrong place, and it takes no descendants with it.
cards.section: Number or place

cards.front: During cortical development, a cortex becomes small but retains orderly layers. Which building step is the first suspect, and why?
cards.back: Neuron production or early survival, because fewer neurons can leave a small cortex even when those present migrate normally.
cards.quote: a small cortex with orderly layers points first to a problem in making neurons (or in their early loss)
cards.section: Number or place

cards.front: In a cortical-growth model, 100 progenitors undergo six symmetric doubling rounds instead of seven. If each progenitor at the switch later makes the same number of neurons, how many progenitors remain, and what is neuron output relative to normal?
cards.back: At the switch: 100 × 2^6 = 6,400 progenitors, versus 100 × 2^7 = 12,800 normally. Neuron output is 6,400/12,800 = 1/2 of normal.
cards.quote: progenitors at the switch = starting progenitors × 2^n, where n is the number of symmetric rounds
cards.section: Number or place

cards.front: In each round of a cortical-growth model, 90% of progenitor divisions yield two progenitors and 10% yield one progenitor plus one neuron. All remaining progenitors can divide again. After ten rounds, what fraction of the normal all-symmetric pool is expected?
cards.back: Mean progenitors per division = 0.90 × 2 + 0.10 × 1 = 1.9. Relative pool = (1.9/2)^10 = 0.95^10 ≈ 0.60, or about 60% of normal.
cards.quote: Each neurogenic division is one progenitor short, so on average a division gives 1.9 progenitors instead of 2, 5 percent short of doubling.
cards.section: Number or place

cards.front: In a growth model with occasional neuron-producing divisions during progenitor expansion, why does total neuron output fall by a smaller fraction than the final progenitor pool?
cards.back: Those divisions already produced some neurons early; a smaller final pool does not count these early neurons.
cards.quote: Those divisions also made a few neurons early, so total neuron output falls a little less than the pool.
cards.section: Number or place

cards.front: What age- and sex-adjusted head-circumference thresholds does the WHO use for microcephaly and severe microcephaly?
cards.back: More than 2 standard deviations below the mean for microcephaly; more than 3 below for severe microcephaly.
cards.quote: The World Health Organization uses a cutoff of more than two standard deviations (SD) below the mean, and calls more than three severe.
cards.section: What a tape measure can tell you

cards.front: Treat a newborn head as a sphere and ignore scalp, skull and fluid. Average circumference is about 34.5 cm, with SD about 1.2 cm. At 2 SD below average, what is the modeled brain volume relative to average?
cards.back: Circumference = 34.5 − 2 × 1.2 = 32.1 cm. Since volume scales as circumference cubed, relative volume = (32.1/34.5)^3 ≈ 0.80, about one-fifth smaller.
cards.quote: treat the head as a sphere, so that head circumference grows as the cube root of brain volume
cards.section: What a tape measure can tell you

cards.front: Why can a head-circumference-based estimate of brain volume not reveal how many progenitor divisions were lost?
cards.back: The model compares volumes, not neuron counts or division histories; head circumference also includes scalp, skull and fluid.
cards.quote: Still, the model only compares volumes; it counts neither neurons nor lost divisions.
cards.section: What a tape measure can tell you

cards.front: Why does a small newborn head not identify a disease or its cause by itself?
cards.back: The cutoff includes some healthy babies, and small heads can result from genes, congenital infections, alcohol or injury around birth.
cards.quote: If head sizes follow a bell curve, about 2 in 100 lie more than 2 SD below the mean.
cards.section: What a tape measure can tell you

cards.front: In recessively inherited primary microcephaly, how many copies of the causal gene must be broken for a child to be affected?
cards.back: Both copies.
cards.quote: inherited as a recessive trait: a child is affected when both copies of a gene are broken.
cards.section: Primary microcephaly: genes at the spindle pole

cards.front: Most primary microcephaly proteins, including ASPM, WDR62 and CDK5RAP2, localize to the centrosome or {{c1::spindle pole}}.
cards.back: These are sites involved in organizing the mitotic spindle.
cards.quote: Most of their proteins sit at the centrosome or the spindle pole.
cards.section: Primary microcephaly: genes at the spindle pole

cards.front: What role do the two centrosomes play during mitosis?
cards.back: They form the poles of the spindle that pulls chromosomes apart.
cards.quote: At mitosis the two centrosomes form the poles of the spindle that pulls the chromosomes apart.
cards.section: Primary microcephaly: genes at the spindle pole

cards.front: How could a tilted spindle change radial glial daughter-cell fates without making fate inevitable?
cards.back: It can distribute the ventricular-facing apical patch unequally. Yet a daughter lacking that patch can still divide as a progenitor away from the ventricle.
cards.quote: The patch does not decide fate on its own: a daughter without it can still divide, as a progenitor away from the ventricle.
cards.section: Why the brain?

cards.front: After Aspm knockdown in mouse embryonic progenitors, division planes tilt and fewer divisions are symmetric and progenitor-making. What mechanism for cortical shrinkage does this support?
cards.back: Reduced expansion of the progenitor pool: altered division orientation accompanies a shift away from divisions that make two progenitors. It supports the spindle hypothesis rather than proving it for every MCPH gene.
cards.quote: knocking down Aspm tilted the plane of progenitor division and shifted divisions away from the symmetric, progenitor-making kind
cards.section: Why the brain?

cards.front: Besides an early switch to neuron-making divisions, how can delayed mitosis reduce the progenitor pool in mouse cortex?
cards.back: Delayed mitosis can trigger p53-dependent cell death, removing progenitors that would otherwise contribute neurons.
cards.quote: in mouse progenitors, delayed mitosis can trigger a death that depends on p53, a protein that senses stress and can halt or kill the cell.
cards.section: Why the brain?

cards.front: Two developing cortices end equally small. One may lose progenitors to early neuron-making divisions; the other to death. What observations during growth would distinguish these mechanisms?
cards.back: Track division outcomes and progenitor deaths against a normal comparison. An early fate shift predicts fewer progenitor-making divisions; a death mechanism predicts more progenitor deaths. Rule: either history can leave fewer neurons, so final size alone cannot distinguish them.
cards.quote: If a fault tips progenitors toward the switch or toward death round after round, it compounds, as in the prediction above.
cards.section: Why the brain?

cards.front: Aspm knockout shrinks ferret cortex more than mouse cortex. Does that establish that extra rounds of division alone cause the species difference? Explain using the proposed mechanisms.
cards.back: No. Extra rounds could amplify a recurring division defect, but early displacement of ventricular radial glia is another compatible explanation. Rule: repeated pool losses compound; this amplification hypothesis does not establish the mechanism of the species difference.
cards.quote: These round counts are illustrative, not measured values for either species, and the reading remains a hypothesis.
cards.section: Why the brain?

cards.front: Why combine epidemiology, fetal pathology and laboratory models when assessing whether Zika causes congenital microcephaly?
cards.back: They connect an outbreak pattern, virus in damaged fetal brain, and a mechanism in susceptible cells. Agreement strengthens causation beyond what any one approach establishes alone.
cards.quote: The case was built from three kinds of evidence pointing the same way.
cards.section: Zika: how do you show that a virus causes a birth defect?

cards.front: Why does microcephaly rising after a Zika outbreak in the same places not establish causation by itself?
cards.back: The pattern is an association; other factors or closer checking of newborns could increase recorded cases.
cards.quote: The rise in microcephaly followed the virus in time and place.
cards.section: Zika: how do you show that a virus causes a birth defect?

cards.front: Zika RNA and virus particles are detected in a small, calcified fetal brain. What does this establish, and what does it leave unresolved?
cards.back: It establishes virus in a damaged fetal brain. This observation alone does not establish that the virus caused the damage or how often such damage occurs.
cards.quote: reported Zika virus RNA and virus particles in the brain of a fetus whose mother had been infected in Brazil during pregnancy.
cards.section: Zika: how do you show that a virus causes a birth defect?

cards.front: Zika-exposed human cortical progenitor cultures show more infection than stem-cell or immature-neuron cultures, with progenitor death and slower growth. Which cortical building step is directly implicated?
cards.back: Neuron production: loss and slowed growth of progenitors reduce the pool available to make neurons. These results directly support a production defect rather than demonstrating a migration defect.
cards.quote: Zika infects human cortical neural progenitors grown from stem cells far more readily than it infects the stem cells or immature neurons
cards.section: Zika: how do you show that a virus causes a birth defect?

cards.front: A Zika progenitor experiment uses an old, repeatedly passaged laboratory strain. What follow-up would address whether its effects apply to the epidemic virus?
cards.back: Repeat the work with epidemic strains. Similar effects would address the concern that the old laboratory strain behaves differently; later organoid and pregnant-mouse work agreed.
cards.quote: An old laboratory strain might not behave like the epidemic virus, so its effect on progenitors might not explain the epidemic.
cards.section: Zika: how do you show that a virus causes a birth defect?

cards.front: Why can a Zika-infected brain organoid demonstrate a possible mechanism without giving the probability of microcephaly in a pregnancy?
cards.back: It shows what the virus can do to human progenitors in a model, not how often that outcome occurs in pregnancies.
cards.quote: it shows what the virus can do to human progenitors, not what it does in each fetus.
cards.section: Zika: how do you show that a virus causes a birth defect?

cards.front: Zika harms progenitors in culture. To study whether pregnancy timing changes microcephaly risk, which human outcome groups would you compare, and why would the culture result alone be insufficient?
cards.back: Compare microcephaly frequency after early infection, later infection and no infection. Rule: model injury shows a possible mechanism, while pregnancy outcomes address risk and timing. Most infected pregnancies do not produce microcephaly, so infection cannot be treated as a certain outcome.
cards.quote: And most infections in pregnancy do not produce microcephaly; the risk appears highest when infection comes early.
cards.section: Zika: how do you show that a virus causes a birth defect?

cards.front: Which developing cortical cell population is especially readily infected by Zika in human stem-cell-derived cultures?
cards.back: Cortical neural progenitors.
cards.quote: Zika infects human cortical neural progenitors grown from stem cells far more readily than it infects the stem cells or immature neurons
cards.section: Zika: how do you show that a virus causes a birth defect?

cards.front: What cortical architecture characterizes classic lissencephaly?
cards.back: A thick cortex with few or no folds, organized into about four crude layers rather than the normal six.
cards.quote: In classic lissencephaly it is thick, has few or no folds, and is organized into about four crude layers.
cards.section: In the wrong place: lissencephaly and the double cortex

cards.front: In a geometric model, a malformed cortex has the same gray-matter volume as normal but four times the thickness. What surface area relative to normal is required?
cards.back: Volume = area × thickness. At equal volume, area ratio = normal thickness/malformed thickness = 1/4 = 25%. This does not establish equal neuron counts because neuron density can differ.
cards.quote: Volume is area times thickness. A smooth cortex about four to five times as thick as normal
cards.section: In the wrong place: lissencephaly and the double cortex

cards.front: What does LIS1 haploinsufficiency mean for neuronal migration?
cards.back: Half the usual LIS1 amount is insufficient for normal migration, even though one normal gene copy remains.
cards.quote: So half the usual amount of LIS1 is too little for neurons to migrate, a state called haploinsufficiency.
cards.section: LIS1: half a dose is not enough

cards.front: A large chromosome deletion removes LIS1 and neighboring genes. A smaller lesion affecting only one LIS1 copy also causes lissencephaly. What does the smaller lesion establish?
cards.back: Loss of one LIS1 copy alone is sufficient to cause lissencephaly. Neighboring-gene loss is not required for that migration disorder, although it may add severity in the larger deletion.
cards.quote: Children who have lost or broken only LIS1, on one copy, still have lissencephaly, called isolated lissencephaly.
cards.section: LIS1: half a dose is not enough

cards.front: Cytoplasmic dynein walks along microtubules toward their {{c1::minus ends}}.
cards.back: Dynein is a motor protein.
cards.quote: cytoplasmic dynein, a motor that walks along microtubules toward their minus ends.
cards.section: LIS1: half a dose is not enough

cards.front: How does a migrating cortical neuron move its nucleus after extending its leading process?
cards.back: Its centrosome advances into the process; dynein pulls the nucleus toward it along microtubules, with help from myosin.
cards.quote: dynein, pulling along microtubules that run back from the centrosome to the nucleus, draws the nucleus up toward it, with help from the motor protein myosin.
cards.section: LIS1: half a dose is not enough

cards.front: After LIS1 knockdown in embryonic rat cortex, a few new cells become bipolar. What happens to leading-process extension and nuclear movement in those cells?
cards.back: Nuclear movement fails despite continued process extension, leaving those neurons short of their layers. This describes the bipolar subset; most new cells failed earlier, remaining multipolar near the ventricle.
cards.quote: In the few that did become bipolar, the leading process kept extending, but the cell body and nucleus barely moved after it.
cards.section: LIS1: half a dose is not enough

cards.front: Doublecortin binds and stabilizes {{c1::microtubules}} in migrating cortical neurons.
cards.back: It is thought mainly to steady the tracks for nuclear movement rather than acting as a motor.
cards.quote: doublecortin, a protein that binds microtubules and stabilizes them in migrating neurons.
cards.section: Doublecortin: one mutation, two brains

cards.front: Why can a female cortex contain lineages of neurons with different X chromosomes active?
cards.back: Each cell randomly silences one X early in development, and its descendants inherit that choice, producing a mosaic.
cards.quote: The choice is inherited by that cell's descendants, so her cortex is a mosaic of neurons with one X or the other active.
cards.section: Doublecortin: one mutation, two brains

cards.front: A female carries a loss-of-function DCX allele on one X chromosome; a male carries it on his sole X. Predict their different cortical malformations and explain why.
cards.back: In the lesson's X-inactivation model, the female can have band heterotopia: mutant-X-active neurons stall beneath a nearly normal cortex. The male has lissencephaly: no neuron makes working doublecortin, so most stall. X inactivation creates the female mosaic; neuron-by-neuron sorting has not been shown in human tissue.
cards.quote: In her mosaic cortex, neurons with the normal X active migrate to the cortex. Neurons with the mutant X active stall partway
cards.section: Doublecortin: one mutation, two brains

cards.front: Silencing DCX in some embryonic rat cortical neurons makes them form a band, but also disturbs some neighboring neurons with DCX intact. How should this affect a claim that DCX acts only within each migrating neuron?
cards.back: Reject the word “only.” Rule: mutant neurons stalling supports an action within those cells, but disturbed intact neighbors allow effects between cells. Female mosaicism fits the within-cell model, yet neuron-by-neuron sorting remains unshown in human tissue.
cards.quote: some neighbouring neurons, with DCX intact, were also disturbed, and the sorting has not been shown neuron by neuron in human tissue.
cards.section: Doublecortin: one mutation, two brains

cards.front: Two fetal cortices end equally small. One made too few neurons; the other made a larger cortex before losing tissue to congenital infection. Can final size identify the original production deficit?
cards.back: No. Rule: final cortical size reflects both production and survival. Tissue destruction can make a cortex small after it was built, so final size cannot by itself reconstruct how many neurons were originally made.
cards.quote: a cortex made and then damaged is small because tissue was lost, not because too few neurons were made.
cards.section: Where the sort breaks

cards.front: To isolate LIS1-dependent migration from LIS1-dependent progenitor division, compare loss restricted to newborn neurons after progenitor division with loss in progenitors and their descendants. Which cortical readouts would distinguish the two roles?
cards.back: Measure neuron production and positioning. Neuron-restricted loss should disrupt placement without directly removing progenitor divisions; progenitor-inclusive loss may reduce production too. Rule: LIS1 supports both nuclear migration and progenitor division, so layer disruption alone cannot establish preserved production.
cards.quote: Real LIS1 loss is messier, because LIS1 also acts in dividing progenitors.
cards.section: Design problem
